section.title: The Law and the Struggle with Sin
section.sectionRationale: Paul has said the law aroused sinful passions, so he must now defend the law itself. Is the law sin? By no means. The law is holy, righteous, and good; yet sin seized the commandment as its opportunity, so that the very commandment meant for life brought death, and sin was exposed as utterly sinful. Then Paul turns to the searching first person account of the divided self, I do not do the good I want but the evil I do not want, warring with indwelling sin, until the cry, wretched man that I am, who will deliver me, breaks into thanks: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
section.thesis: The law is not sin but holy, righteous, and good; it exposes and provokes sin without power to save, and the honest anatomy of the divided self, delighting in God's law yet held captive to indwelling sin, drives the believer from every hope in self to cry for deliverance and to give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the law is not sin but exposes it; the commandment meant for life brought death, yet the law is holy; the struggle of the divided self with indwelling sin; and the cry of the wretched man answered by thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.label: Is the law sin?
units.note: the law reveals and exposes sin

verses.text: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law. For I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, “Do not covet.”
But {{hamartia|sin}}, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead.

units.label: The commandment meant for life brought death
units.note: yet the law is holy, righteous, and good

verses.text: Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died.
So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death.
For sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death.
So then, the {{nomos|law}} is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.

units.label: Sin exposed as utterly sinful
units.note: good turned to death that sin might be seen

verses.text: Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! But in order that sin might be exposed as sin, it produced death in me through what was good, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.

units.label: The divided self
units.note: I do not do the good I want

verses.text: We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.
I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.
And if I do what I do not want to do, I admit that the law is good.
In that case, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.
I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my {{sarx|flesh}}; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.
For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.
And if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.

units.label: Wretched man that I am
units.note: who will deliver me? Thanks be to God

verses.text: So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.
For in my {{eso_anthropos|inner being}} I delight in God’s law.
But I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me.
What a {{talaiporos|wretched}} man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?
Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

nomos.gloss: Law, the law of Moses. Paul defends it emphatically: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. The problem is never the law itself but sin, which abuses the good commandment. The law reveals God's will and exposes sin, yet it cannot give the power to obey; it diagnoses the disease it cannot cure.

hamartia.gloss: Sin, here almost personified as an active, deceiving power that seizes its opportunity through the commandment. Sin uses even the good law as a base of operations, provoking the very desire the law forbids. Paul shows sin to be so malignant that it turns the good commandment into an occasion for death, so that sin might be seen as utterly sinful.

sarx.gloss: Flesh, human nature in its fallen weakness and bent toward sin. Paul says nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; the flesh is the foothold of indwelling sin, so that even the desire to do good is frustrated in its carrying out. The struggle of the passage is the struggle against sin still lodged in the flesh.

eso_anthropos.gloss: The inner being or inner man, the deepest self renewed to delight in God. Paul says in my inner being I delight in God's law, describing a genuine, heartfelt love for what God commands. This inward delight, at war with the law of sin in the members, is characteristic of one whose heart has been renewed toward God.

talaiporos.gloss: Wretched, miserable, worn out by struggle. Paul's cry, what a wretched man I am, is the anguished honesty of one who feels the weight of indwelling sin and longs for full deliverance. It is not despair but a groan that gives way at once to thanks to God, who delivers through Jesus Christ our Lord.

basic.context: Paul has just said the law aroused sinful passions, which could make the law sound evil. So he asks, is the law sin? His answer is an emphatic no. The law is good; it shows us what sin is. But sin seizes the good commandment and uses it against us. Then Paul opens up the inner struggle: I want to do good, but I keep doing the evil I hate.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the passage in two parts. First, verses 7 to 13 defend the law and expose sin's malice. Second, verses 14 to 25 give a searching first person account of the divided self at war with indwelling sin. There is a long standing debate about who the I is, but the passage clearly aims to humble every hope in self and to drive us to Christ, ending in thanks to God through Him.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul defends the nomos, the law, as holy and good. The villain is hamartia, sin, an active power that abuses the commandment. Nothing good dwells in the sarx, the flesh, yet in the eso anthropos, the inner being, Paul delights in God's law. The struggle drives him to cry talaiporos, wretched, before bursting into thanks to God through Jesus Christ.
basic.typology: The cry for deliverance from this body of death echoes Israel's groaning in bondage, answered by the exodus, and points forward to the redemption of the body at the resurrection. The good law that could not give life foreshadows the greater work of Christ and the Spirit, who accomplish what the law revealed but could not achieve.
basic.christ: The whole struggle drives to Christ. The question who will rescue me is answered in the next breath: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Only He delivers from the body of death. The law could expose the disease, but Christ alone is the cure, and the chapter's anguished honesty is meant to send us to Him and to the life in the Spirit that Romans 8 unfolds.
basic.god: God gave the law, which is holy, righteous, and good, a reflection of His own character. God is the one to whom Paul gives thanks for deliverance through His Son. The passage guards God's goodness in giving the law while exposing the depth of human sin, so that all the glory of rescue belongs to God alone through Jesus Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 answers this chapter: what the law could not do, God did by sending His Son and His Spirit. Galatians 5 describes the flesh and the Spirit in conflict. Romans 3 says through the law comes the knowledge of sin. Exodus 20 gives the commandment, Do not covet, that Paul cites.
basic.oneStory: The Bible shows a good law given by a good God, meeting a people unable to keep it, so that sin is exposed and every mouth stopped. This chapter voices that predicament at its most personal, the divided heart crying for rescue. The story does not end in the groan but in the thanks, for God delivers through Jesus Christ our Lord, and Romans 8 opens with no condemnation and life in the Spirit.

context.literary:
Romans 7:7-25 is a single piece of argument in two halves, and the change of tense marks the seam. Verses 7 to 13 are told mostly in the past, a story of an 'I' who was once alive, met a commandment and died. Verses 14 to 25 shift into the present tense, and the same 'I' now stands in a courtroom and in a battlefield. The first half defends the law; the second half laments the person. Between them Paul asks the same question twice, 'Is the law sin?' in verse 7 and 'Did that which is good, then, become death to me?' in verse 13, and he gives it the same answer, 'Certainly not!'

Sin is the subject of almost every action in the first half. It seizes its opportunity, produces covetousness, springs to life, deceives and kills, verses 8 to 11. The law only commands, and the commandment is only the thing sin uses. In the second half the 'I' takes over the verbs, but the refrain of verses 17 and 20 pushes the agency back to 'sin living in me', and those two verses are word for word identical. Verses 15 and 16 and 19 and 20 are variations on one thought, so the passage moves in circles, as the experience it describes does.

The word 'law' itself changes meaning. In verses 22 to 25 Paul speaks of the law of God, the law of my mind, 'another law' in the members and the law of sin, a play on the word that makes the war a war of principles as well as persons. The passage ends on a cry, verse 24, a thanksgiving, verse 25a, and a summary, verse 25b. The thanksgiving seems to come early, and the summary of the divided self returns after it. Paul has deliberately left the tension unresolved until Romans 8:1, 'there is now no condemnation', where the answer begins.
context.historical:
The 'I' of Romans 7 spoke into a world that had its own accounts of the divided self. Greek thinkers argued over whether anyone could know the good and still do evil, and called the condition akrasia, a failure of self-command. The tragic figure of Medea, in Ovid's Latin, says that she sees the better and approves it but follows the worse. Paul's readers would have recognized the experience, and some would have tried to read him as one more philosopher of weak will.

Paul does not describe weakness of will. His problem is not ignorance, since the person sees and approves the good, and it is not a lack of resolve alone, since the person wants to do right. His diagnosis is that there is an active power at work in the members. Jewish thought had an equivalent concept. Genesis 6:5 speaks of the inclination of the thoughts of the human heart as altogether evil, and the Hebrew word for 'inclination', yetser, later gave rise to the teaching about an evil impulse in every person. Paul's picture is of a person who delights in the Torah and cannot keep it.

Paul himself was a man of whom this sounds strange, because he said he had been faultless as to righteousness in the law, Philippians 3:6. The tenth commandment, 'Do not covet', is the one commandment that cannot be kept by outward conduct, since it is about desire. Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21 both give it, and the BSB footnote on Romans 7:7 points to both. A zealous Pharisee could measure himself against the other nine by his actions. The tenth would have shown him his heart.

The church in Rome was dealing with the question of the law from both sides, with Jewish believers who loved the Torah and Gentile believers who had never been under it. In this setting Paul needed to defend the law's goodness against the charge of Gentile critics, and to deny its power to save against the hope of Jewish ones.
context.canonical:
Romans 7 is an exposition of ideas laid down earlier in the same letter. Romans 3:20 said that through the law comes the knowledge of sin, and Romans 4:15 that where there is no law there is no transgression, and Romans 5:20 that the law came in so that the trespass would increase. Chapter 7 shows how this works in a single life. Behind it lies Genesis 2:17 and 3:13, where a commandment is followed by deceit and death.

The rest of Paul's writing echoes the passage. Galatians 5:17 describes the flesh and the Spirit as opposed to each other 'so that you do not do what you want', and 1 Corinthians 15:56 says 'the power of sin is the law'. Galatians 3:19 asks why the law was given and answers that it was added because of transgressions, and Galatians 3:22 that Scripture confined all things under sin. First Timothy 1:8 supplies the other half of the picture: 'the law is good, if one uses it legitimately'. In 1 Timothy 1:15 Paul calls himself, in the present tense, the worst of sinners. First John 1:8-10 tells believers who say they have no sin that they deceive themselves, and promises forgiveness to those who confess.

The psalms are the passage's natural companions. The 'I' who delights in God's law in his inner being could be speaking Psalm 119:97, and the one who has no hope before God's judgment could be praying Psalm 143:2.

The interpretation of the passage has shaped the history of the church. The earlier Greek fathers tended to read it as the unrenewed person, and the later Augustine, followed by Luther and Calvin, as the believer. Wesleyan and many other traditions have read it as the person under the law before Christ. The debate is set out in the next section, but all agree that Romans 8 answers the cry of 7:24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul has said that the law aroused sinful passions, and he knows how that sounds. He answers by taking the law's side with every word he has, calling it holy, righteous, good and spiritual. The first thing he wants the Romans to understand is that the trouble lies elsewhere. The law is a mirror and a measure. It shows sin as sin, and it does not give strength.

He then turns the lamp on the person. He had to describe, with painful accuracy, what life under the commandment feels like to someone who truly wants God's will. The aim is not despair for its own sake. It is to take away every last hope that effort, education, sincerity or a good conscience can do the work of rescue. A reader who sees the 'I' in this chapter, wanting the good and failing to do it, is meant to join in the cry of verse 24 and so to be ready for verse 25.

Finally, Paul wanted his readers to take the thanks of verse 25 seriously. He answers the question 'who will rescue me?' with a name and a gratitude, and then holds the unfinished struggle open one more sentence. He wanted them to know that the cure is not a better will but a person, and that its fullness waits for Romans 8.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is an anatomy and not a set of rules. Paul reports what happens when sin meets the law in a human heart, and he offers no instruction to follow. The closest thing to a command is the lesson of the whole, that we should not look to the law as a source of life, and not look to ourselves as the solution.

That matters for how the passage is used. It is sometimes read as a license, as if 'it is no longer I who do it' removed responsibility. Paul does not say that. The 'I' still wants the good, hates the evil and admits the law is good, and the verses that put the doing on 'sin living in me' are not an excuse but a diagnosis of where the real enemy is. The 'I' still says 'wretched man that I am'.

It is also sometimes read as a pattern for the Christian life in which defeat is normal. The passage does not say that either. Paul does not hold it up as the ideal, and Romans 8:2-4 is his answer to it. Believers can learn from the passage that they will meet the pull of sin and that their joy in the law is a sign of a new heart. They are not told that this is the best they can expect. The New Testament elsewhere speaks of real victories, Romans 8:13, and of a continuing fight, Galatians 5:17, and the reader must hold both.

debates.question: Who is the 'I' of verses 7 to 13, the part told in the past tense?

views.label: Adam meeting the commandment
views.case: Verses 9 to 11 sound like Genesis 2 and 3. There was a time when 'I was alive apart from the law', then a commandment arrived, then sin seized its opportunity through it, 'deceived me' and put me to death. Genesis 3:13 has Eve say, 'The serpent deceived me', and Paul uses the same family of words of Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3. On this reading the 'I' is the first human being, and so every human being in him, Romans 5:12.

views.label: Israel receiving the law at Sinai
views.case: Others hear Israel at the mountain. The people were redeemed and 'alive' before the law came, and the commandment then exposed the sin in them, culminating at the golden calf. This fits Paul's concern in the surrounding chapters with the place of the law in Israel's story, and with Romans 5:20, where the law came in so that the trespass would increase.

views.label: Paul's own experience, and everyone's
views.case: Some stay closer to the first person and see Paul speaking for himself as one who once thought himself blameless, Philippians 3:6, until the tenth commandment found him out. A Greek writer could also speak in an imagined voice, so the 'I' may be a representative one that includes the reader. The three need not be exclusive.

debates.bearing: Whichever figure stands behind the 'I', the content is the same: the law arrives, shows what sin is, and finds sin already at home, using the holy command for its own purpose. Reading the story as Adam's, Israel's and one's own at once makes the point that every person re-enacts the first sin when meeting a good command.

debates.question: Who is the I in Romans 7:14 to 25?

views.label: The regenerate believer's ongoing struggle with indwelling sin
views.case: The historic Reformed reading, held by the later Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, notes the present tense, the delight in God's law in the inner being, the hatred of sin, and the will toward good, which fit a renewed heart, not an unbeliever; the passage describes the real and continuing battle of the Christian against sin still lodged in the flesh, a battle answered by the Spirit in chapter 8.

views.label: The unregenerate person, or Paul under the law before Christ
views.case: Others take the I as the person under the law apart from Christ, sold as a slave to sin and unable to do good, arguing that the defeated tone and the captivity to sin do not match the freedom of chapter 6 or the victory of chapter 8; on this view Paul dramatizes life under the law before the Spirit's liberation.

views.label: Israel, or Adam, or a rhetorical everyman under the law
views.case: Some read the I representatively, as Israel meeting the law at Sinai, or Adam meeting the commandment in Eden, or humanity in general under the law, using the first person as a vivid rhetorical device rather than strict autobiography.

debates.bearing: Foregrounding the regenerate reading, the passage gives sober comfort: even the true Christian wages a lifelong war with indwelling sin, yet is not condemned, for deliverance is sure through Jesus Christ and the Spirit; the other readings rightly warn that the law cannot save and that the flesh profits nothing, and all agree the answer is not self effort but Christ.

debates.question: How can the law be good if it brought death?

views.label: The fault lies in sin, not in the law
views.case: The historic reading holds that the law is holy, righteous, and good, and that sin, not the law, produced death by abusing the good commandment; the law rightly exposes and even provokes sin so that sin is seen as utterly sinful.

views.label: The law itself is a defective or enslaving power
views.case: Some speak as though the law itself is the problem to be escaped; but Paul explicitly clears the law of blame, laying the guilt on indwelling sin, so that the law's goodness stands even as it cannot give life.

debates.bearing: Keeping the blame on sin rather than the law honors God, who gave the law, and clarifies the gospel: the law is a good diagnosis that cannot cure, so salvation must come from Christ and the Spirit, not from the law.

study.originalLanguages:
The sin that 'seized its opportunity' in verses 8 and 11 is working through a word with a military feel, aphorme. It means a starting point or base of operations, the place from which an attack is launched. Paul uses the same word in Galatians 5:13 for freedom turned into 'an opportunity for the flesh'. Sin does not need the law to be evil, only to be near, and the commandment becomes the fortress from which sin strikes. The verb 'produced' in verse 8 and 'produced' in verse 13 is a related one, katergazomai, which Paul repeats in verses 15, 17, 18 and 20. It means to work something out to completion, and it is the verb for what sin does in me and for what I fail to do. Sin brings to completion what the law cannot.

In verse 9 sin 'sprang to life'. The Greek is anezesen, a compound that means to come alive again, as the prodigal son was 'alive again' in Luke 15:24. Verse 8 says that 'apart from the law, sin is dead', which means dormant, not absent. The first death in the verse, sin's, is a sleep. The second, mine, is real.

The verb 'deceived' in verse 11 is exapatao. Paul uses the same verb of the serpent's treatment of Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3, and 1 Timothy 2:14 uses it of Eve too. The Greek version of Genesis 3:13 has the simple form of the same verb. The echo is quiet but it is there: the commandment, the deceit, the death, the pattern of the garden repeated.

In verse 14 the contrast is between the law, 'spiritual', and the speaker, who is sarkinos. The word is formed to mean made of flesh, and it speaks of the speaker's whole constitution as earthly, not just a lapse. 'Sold as a slave to sin' is a perfect participle, pepramenos, a state that was entered and remains. The language of being sold recalls how the prophets described Israel, 'you were sold for your iniquities', Isaiah 50:1, and Ahab, who 'sold himself to do evil', 1 Kings 21:25.

Verse 15 says that the speaker does not 'understand', and the Greek verb is ginosko, to know or recognize. The speaker cannot recognize his own behaviour as his own. The sentence 'what I want to do, I do not do' states the problem, and verse 18 states the cause, that nothing good lives in the flesh.

The two sides of the self in verses 22 and 23 are 'the inner being' and 'the members'. 'Inner being' is Paul's phrase for the person as God sees him, and he uses it in Ephesians 3:16 for what the Spirit strengthens and in 2 Corinthians 4:16 for what is 'renewed day by day'. 'Members' is melos, the same word as the 'parts of your body' offered to God in 6:13 and 6:19. The war is waged in the very limbs that were to serve righteousness. The two verbs of the war, 'warring against' and 'holding me captive', are antistrateuomai and aichmalotizo, the first a campaign, the second the taking of a prisoner. Paul uses the second again in 2 Corinthians 10:5 when he says we 'take captive every thought'.

The cry of verse 24 is 'wretched', talaiporos, a word that appears again in the Lord's letter to Laodicea, Revelation 3:17, where it names a state that the church was too complacent to notice. 'Who will rescue me' uses a verb, rhuomai, that Paul takes up in 11:26 of the Deliverer who comes from Zion, and in 1 Thessalonians 1:10, Jesus 'our deliverer from the coming wrath'. 'This body of death' may mean the body doomed to die, or the body as the seat of sin's rule, as in 'the body of sin' of 6:6. Paul keeps both in play, and Romans 8:23 will answer with 'the redemption of our bodies'.

typology.fulfillment: At the exodus God heard the groaning of Israel in Egypt and sent a deliverer. The cry of verse 24 stands in the same line: the groaning of a people who cannot free themselves, answered not by their own strength but by a rescuer. Paul does not call the passage an allegory of Israel in Egypt, but the shape of the situation recalls it, and Christ is the Deliverer who is named at the end, Romans 11:26 and 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The type falls short where Egypt's chains were external and the deliverance could be a march out of a land; the bondage of Romans 7 is in the members, and the rescue must be worked inside the person.

Leviticus 18:5 says that the person who keeps God's statutes will live by them, and Paul quotes it in Romans 10:5. In Romans 7:10 he says that the commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death. The good law is a promise of life to anyone who can keep it, and Christ is the one person who did, Hebrews 4:15, so that He could bring the life the law promised, John 5:39-40. The pattern falls short in that the law could promise life but never provide the power to obey; the life it pointed to arrived in a Person.

typology.type: The delight in the law, from the Psalms to the Son
typology.fulfillment: The righteous man of Psalm 1 delights in the law of the LORD, and the psalmist of 119:97 cries, 'Oh, how I love Your law!' The 'I' of Romans 7:22 shares that delight. Psalm 40:8, which Hebrews 10:7 puts in the mouth of Christ, says, 'I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.' In Him the delight and the deed were joined. The type falls short because the psalmist's delight was real but his obedience incomplete, whereas in Christ the pattern is finished and then made available to His people by the Spirit, Romans 8:4.

typology.type: The body of death and the redeemed body
typology.fulfillment: Paul's longing for rescue from 'this body of death' looks forward to the day when the body itself will be changed. Romans 8:23 speaks of waiting for 'the redemption of our bodies', and Philippians 3:21 says Christ 'will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body'. The first fruits of that hope are already given in the Spirit, and the hope is secured by the risen body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The type falls short in the present, because the body is not yet redeemed and the believer lives between the first fruits and the harvest.

study.christ:
Christ is named only once in the whole passage, in the last verse, but the entire passage is built to make His name necessary. Paul asks a 'who' question, 'Who will rescue me?', and the answer is a name, Jesus Christ our Lord. Every other candidate has been ruled out. The law has been shown to be unable, the will has been shown to be willing but unable, and the flesh has been shown to be beyond improvement. The deliverer must come from outside the speaker, as the Deliverer who comes from Zion in Romans 11:26 comes from outside the people He saves.

The passage leads to Christ by contrast. The 'I' of chapter 7 wants the good and does not do it. Christ is the one who could say, in the words of Psalm 40:8 as Hebrews 10:5-7 gives them, 'I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.' He met the same law and the same kinds of temptation, but where the commandment gave sin its opportunity in every other human being, in Him it found no foothold. He was tempted in every way and was without sin, Hebrews 4:15, and in the wilderness He answered the tempter from the commandments, Matthew 4:4. The only person to whom the law was ever what it was meant to be, a way of life, is the one who rescues the rest.

It leads to Christ by the cross. What the law could not do, Paul says in 8:3, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, and He condemned sin in the flesh. The same flesh in which sin ruled the speaker of chapter 7 was taken by the Son, who did not sin in it and in His death carried its penalty. Galatians 3:13 adds that He became a curse for those under the law. Where the law's curse had fallen on the failing 'I', it fell on Him.

It leads to Christ by the resurrection. The body of death receives its answer in His body, raised, and in the promise that He will 'transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body', Philippians 3:21. First Corinthians 15:57 sounds the same note of thanksgiving as Romans 7:25: 'thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ'. The passage's thanks are therefore not for an idea but for a person who is risen.

We should be careful of two mistakes. The first is to treat the 'I' as a type of Christ, which it is not; the 'I' is the one who needs rescue. The second is to make the commandment about coveting a hidden picture of Christ. The links above are those the New Testament itself makes, and they are sufficient. Christ does not appear in verses 7 to 24 as a figure in a code. He appears at the end as the answer.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He gave the law and that the law is good. Paul will not let anyone blame God for what sin does with it. 'The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good,' verse 12. The psalmist had said the same, 'The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul', Psalm 19:7. A God whose command can be misused by sin, but who is never the author of the misuse, is a God whose goodness stands above the failure of those who receive His word.

The second is that He uses what is good to expose what is evil. Verse 13 says that sin 'produced death in me through what was good' in order that sin might be exposed as sin and become utterly sinful. The purpose clause says that this exposure is not an accident. God's gift of the law has this effect on purpose, to bring sin into the light so that it can be named and dealt with. Galatians 3:22 says Scripture confined everything under sin, and Romans 11:32 gives the aim: 'so that He may have mercy on everyone'. The plan reaches through the darkness of this chapter to mercy.

The third is that God knows the heart. The delight in His law that the speaker feels, and the hatred of sin, are visible to Him in a way they are not to men. The psalmist's prayer, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart', Psalm 139:23, is the prayer that the passage invites. He does not despise the speaker's cry; He answers it. The thanksgiving of verse 25 is directed to God, who is the one who has rescued.

The fourth is that God is the rescuer. The word rhuomai is used of God's saving acts elsewhere, and the sentence 'Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord' puts the work in His hands and the credit in His. The believer's confidence is not in the strength of the delight but in the faithfulness of the Deliverer.

For worship, the passage teaches honesty. A person who has read verses 15 to 24 can pray without pretending, confess without excuse, and give thanks without boasting. It also teaches that gratitude is the end of the struggle and not its price. The one who is divided in himself is not abandoned. God has acted, and the sentence of the next chapter, 'there is now no condemnation', is the Father's answer to the wretched man.

There is a tension the passage holds and does not resolve. God is sovereign and the law is His, yet the human being is truly responsible, saying 'I admit that the law is good', and truly in bondage, saying 'sold as a slave to sin'. Paul leaves both standing and points to the God who has acted.

crossReferences.note: The law merely brings awareness of sin. This is the thesis that Romans 7:7 illustrates with the tenth commandment: Paul would not have known what covetousness was without the law. The one verse states the principle and the other puts it in the first person.

The law came in so that the trespass would increase, though grace increased all the more. Romans 7:8-13 shows the way the increase occurs, with sin finding an opportunity in the commandment, and the grace of 8:1 is the all the more of the same sentence.

The commandment Paul cites is the tenth word of the Decalogue, which forbids coveting. It is the only one of the ten that addresses desire, not deed, and so it is the one that could not be kept by outward conformity, as Paul's sudden awareness of his own heart shows.

The woman answers God, 'The serpent deceived me.' Paul says that sin 'deceived me' through the commandment, and in 2 Corinthians 11:3 he uses the same verb as Genesis for the serpent's work on Eve. The garden pattern of command, deceit and death is the pattern of Romans 7:11.

The flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, so that you do not do what you want. This is the closest parallel to the conflict of verses 15 to 23, but Galatians pairs it with the instruction to walk by the Spirit, which points toward the resolution of Romans 8.

Paul's testimony that he was faultless as to righteousness in the law, and that he came to count it all as loss for the sake of Christ and a righteousness that is through faith. It shows how a good conscience under the law could coexist with the blindness that Romans 7 exposes.

The speaker delights to do God's will with the law within his heart. Hebrews 10:5-7 puts these words on the lips of Christ. The delight of the 'I' in Romans 7:22 is the delight of a person who has been given a new heart, and the delight of the Son was never divided.

Paul says the law is good if used legitimately, and then calls himself the worst of sinners, to whom Christ Jesus came in mercy. The same two truths of Romans 7, the goodness of the law and the depth of sin, sit together in a single paragraph.

To say we have no sin is to deceive ourselves, but if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us. John gives the pastoral side of what Romans 7 describes: sin is real in the believer's life, and the response is honest confession to a faithful God.

The answer to the passage. No condemnation, and the law of the Spirit of life has set believers free from the law of sin and death. What the law could not do, God has done in His Son, so that the righteous standard of the law may be fulfilled in us.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story has a commandment at its centre from the start. In the garden there was one prohibition, and the serpent turned it into an occasion for distrust, Genesis 3:1-6. Paul's account of what happened to the 'I' in Romans 7:9-11 is the same story told in the first person: a command arrives, sin finds an opening, a lie is believed, and death follows. The failure of the first human being is reproduced in every human heart that meets a command.

When God gave the law to Israel the story of the garden took a second turn. The people were redeemed first, and then given the word that would show them how to live, and from the golden calf onward they showed what their hearts were made of. The history of Israel is a long demonstration that a good law given to a people with an unchanged heart does not produce righteousness. The prophets saw it, Jeremiah 17:9, and they looked for something deeper. A new covenant, a new heart and a new Spirit were promised, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26-27, so that the people might do what the law required.

Romans 7:7-25 describes the situation that made that promise necessary. The delight in the law, which God has given to His own, is real, and so is the failure. This is the place the story reaches before the cross: the people of God longing to obey and unable to, and a world that groans with them. At the end of the chapter the answer is a name, and the story turns on it. Christ enters the same human condition, fulfils the commandment and takes its curse. The Spirit, whom the next chapter introduces, begins to write the law on the heart.

The story does not end with the resolution of the first fruits. Romans 8:23 says that believers groan inwardly while they wait for the redemption of their bodies, and the struggle of Romans 7 is the struggle of a people between the first fruits and the harvest. Revelation 21:27 and 22:3 describe the end of that story, a city where nothing unclean enters and there is no longer any curse. The 'I' of Romans 7, wretched and divided, becomes in that city one of the servants who see His face, and the law that once exposed them is written on hearts that cannot but love it, as in the prophecy of Jeremiah 31:33.

quiz.q: How does Paul answer the question, is the law sin?

options.text: Certainly not; the law is holy, righteous, and good, and it exposes sin.
options.note: Paul clears the law of blame and lays the fault on sin.

options.text: Yes, the law is itself a sinful and enslaving power.
options.note: Paul emphatically denies this; the law is holy and good.

options.text: The law is neither good nor bad, simply irrelevant.
options.note: Paul insists the law is positively good, not neutral.

options.text: The law is good only for unbelievers.
options.note: The law does expose sin, but Paul insists it is good in itself for all, not merely useful for one audience.

quiz.q: How did sin use the good commandment, according to Paul?

options.text: Sin seized the commandment as an opportunity and produced covetous desire.
options.note: Sin abuses the good law, provoking the very desire it forbids.

options.text: Sin obeyed the commandment and became good.
options.note: Sin does not obey; it exploits the commandment against us.

options.text: Sin ignored the commandment entirely.
options.note: Sin did not ignore it; it seized it as a base of operations.

options.text: Sin was created by the commandment.
options.note: The commandment reveals and provokes sin, but does not create it; sin seizes the law as its opportunity.

quiz.q: What does the struggle I do not do the good I want reveal?

options.text: The reality of indwelling sin warring against the desire to do good.
options.note: The divided self shows sin still lodged in the flesh.

options.text: That the desire to do good is enough to guarantee doing it.
options.note: There is a real desire for good, but the passage shows desire alone does not guarantee the deed, for indwelling sin frustrates it.

options.text: That doing good is actually easy for everyone.
options.note: The passage shows the opposite, the frustration of the will by sin.

options.text: That the law is to blame for the failure.
options.note: Paul blames indwelling sin, not the law, which he calls good.

quiz.q: In the historic Reformed reading, who is the I of Romans 7:14 to 25?

options.text: The regenerate believer in ongoing struggle with indwelling sin.
options.note: Augustine, Luther, and Calvin read the delight in God's law and hatred of sin as marks of a renewed heart.

options.text: Paul under the law before Christ, or the unregenerate person.
options.note: A serious and fairly held view that stresses defeat under the law, though the historic reading foregrounds the believer's struggle.

options.text: Israel or Adam as a purely rhetorical everyman.
options.note: A representative reading exists, but it tends to loosen the personal force the passage carries.

options.text: A sinless person with no real battle against sin.
options.note: The passage is defined by struggle; it cannot describe a sinless life.

quiz.q: How is the cry, who will rescue me from this body of death, answered?

options.text: Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
options.note: Deliverance comes not from self effort but from God through Christ.

options.text: By trying harder to keep the law.
options.note: This is the natural instinct, but the passage shows law keeping cannot deliver; rescue is through Christ alone.

options.text: By concluding that no rescue is possible.
options.note: The cry gives way at once to thanksgiving for real deliverance.

options.text: By escaping the body through mystical experience.
options.note: Deliverance is through Jesus Christ, not through escaping the body by mysticism.

questions: Paul insists the law is holy, righteous, and good, yet it cannot give the power to obey. How does this change what you expect from rules and resolutions in your own life?
Sin seizes even good commandments as an opportunity. Where have you seen a good boundary actually provoke the very desire it forbids in your heart?
The believer delights in God's law in the inner being yet still battles indwelling sin. How does it comfort you to know that this struggle is normal to the Christian life?
Paul cries wretched man that I am before giving thanks to God. Why is honest lament over remaining sin a healthy part of the Christian walk rather than a sign of failure?
The rescue comes through Jesus Christ our Lord, not through self effort. Where are you tempted to fight sin by willpower alone rather than looking to Christ and the Spirit?

translationNotes.note: Once I was alive apart from the law is variously understood, whether of Paul's own experience, of humanity in Adam, or of Israel before Sinai; it describes a former state of seeming life before the commandment brought the knowledge and power of sin to light.

Nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh, uses sarx for fallen human nature; Paul qualifies the statement with that is, in my flesh, since he also speaks of an inner being that delights in God's law.

The verse contains a line break in the source, rendered here as a single space: the thanksgiving through Jesus Christ our Lord is followed by the summary that with the mind Paul serves God's law but with the flesh the law of sin.
